references.text: Joseph's brothers planned to kill him to get rid of the heir, just as the vineyard workers in the parable plan to kill the heir: 'Come, let us kill him' ([ref:1 Mos 37:20|Genesis 37:20]).

The psalm about the Messiah-king who will receive the nations as an inheritance – 'the inheritance' (κληρονομία) that the vineyard workers seek to seize, corresponds to the inheritance God promises his Son ([ref:Sal 2:8|Psalm 2:8]).

Isaiah's song about the vineyard is the background for the entire parable. The owner of the vineyard expects fruit but is disappointed. In [ref:Jes 5:1-7|Isaiah 5:1-7], the vineyard represents Israel, and God is the owner – the same image Jesus uses.

The parallel passage in Matthew: 'But when the vineyard workers saw the son, they said to one another, "Here comes the heir. Come, let us kill him and take his inheritance!"' ([ref:Matt 21:38|Matthew 21:38]).
The parallel passage in Mark: 'But the vineyard workers said to each other, "Here comes the heir. Come, let us kill him, so that the inheritance will be ours!"' ([ref:Mark 12:7|Mark 12:7]).
The son is 'the heir' (κληρονόμος) – Hebrews confirms that God has appointed the Son as heir of all things ([ref:Hebr 1:2|Hebrews 1:2]).
Stephen accuses the Jewish leaders of following the same pattern as the vineyard workers – they persecuted the prophets and finally killed 'the Righteous One' ([ref:Apg 7:51-52|Acts 7:51-52]).

The fulfillment of the parable: Herod, Pilate, the Gentile nations, and the tribes of Israel gathered against God's 'holy servant Jesus' – just as the vineyard workers planned to kill the heir ([ref:Apg 4:27-28|Acts 4:27-28]).
Korah's rebellion against Moses and Aaron reflects the same pattern: rebelling against the one God has appointed in order to seize authority ([ref:4 Mos 16:3|Numbers 16:3]).
